about: What bench/bench.py runs with --plan bench/plan-autopilot.json: smock under the resources of the smallest general-purpose GKE Autopilot Pods and of the Helm chart's default, simulated on this machine with the same cgroup limits. Each profile is a CPU limit, a CFS quota over a 100 ms period as Kubernetes sets for a CPU limit equal to the request, and a memory limit, memory.max, with no swap. autopilot-burst-min is the smallest Pod where Pods may burst (50m CPU, 52 MiB); autopilot-min the smallest where they may not (250m, 512 MiB); chart-default the Helm chart's default requests and limits (1 CPU, 1 GiB), which Autopilot accepts as they are. smock runs with its defaults, the Journal's bounds included, so a profile too small for them shows as OOM kills. Each case climbs a ladder of fixed rates, one step each, from the lowest: the same ladder for each profile in proportion to its CPU limit, 2,500 to 80,000 requests a second per CPU, whose top is about where smock uses up its CPU over HTTPS. That ladder has the rates of the targets in bench/targets.json for amd64 (125 under 50m, 1,250 under 250m and 10,000 under 1 CPU), and those of arm64 under 50m and 250m (250 under 50m, 5,000 under 250m). http-keep-alive's ladder also has 30,000 a second per CPU, for arm64's target of 30,000 under 1 CPU, and 50,000 a second per CPU, by which smock had used up its CPU under each profile in the GKE Autopilot probe the arm64 targets come from. h2c-keep-alive and h2-keep-alive are http-keep-alive over HTTP/2, with its ladders and its targets: h2c to the plain port by prior knowledge, and h2 to the TLS port, which oha offers alone by ALPN, one request at a time on each connection (oha's -p 1). oha cannot open a new connection for each request over HTTP/2, so only keep-alive cases have HTTP/2 twins. With one request at a time, no connection carries two streams at once, so h2c-multiplexed measures smock serving many streams on each connection: h2c with http-keep-alive's ladders over 16 connections, split by weight as in the other cases, each carrying 4 requests at once (oha's -p 4), so that about 64 are in flight, as in the others. It has no targets, and runs only on one machine (local_only): the GKE run leaves it out. Otherwise as bench/plan.json: the window, the request mix, the 64 connections of every other case. idle_rss is smock's RSS settle_s seconds after it is ready under each profile, before any load. The targets of bench/targets.json hold under these profiles, by name and limits.
note: Simulated on this machine: smock's CPU quota and memory limit are those of the profile, but its CPU is this machine's, not the one GKE schedules the Pod on, and the load comes over loopback, not a Pod network. Absolute numbers differ from GKE's; compare profiles, and runs on the same machine.
